Minimum Risk Point Estimation of the Location of a Negative Exponential Distribution

Source: R/seq_mr_nexp_mean.R
seq_mr_nexp_mean.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) procedure for the location parameter of a negative exponential distribution (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009). The negative exponential (two parameter exponential) distribution has density \(\sigma^{-1}\exp\{-(x - \theta)/\sigma\}\) for \(x > \theta\): \(\theta\) is the location, the smallest value the variable can take (a minimum response time, a guarantee period), and \(\sigma\) is the scale. Despite the function's name, the quantity estimated is the location \(\theta\), not the mean (which is \(\theta + \sigma\)). The procedure is risk based, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

seq_mr_nexp_mean(x, A, c, k, t, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 2).

A

The loss constant: the price of one unit of estimation error raised to the power k, in the same currency as c. A positive number.

c

The cost constant: sampling \(n\) observations costs \(c\,n^t\). A positive number.

k

The power applied to the estimation error in the loss: 1 for absolute error, 2 for squared error. Any positive number.

t

The power applied to the sample size in the cost: 1 when each observation costs the same, more than 1 when later observations cost more. Any positive number.

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

location

The sample minimum, the point estimate of the location \(\theta\).

risk

The estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A\,\Gamma(k+1)\,(U_n/n)^k + c\,n^t\).

optimal_n

The sample size the current scale estimate calls for, \(\lceil \{A\,k\,\Gamma(k+1)\,U_n^k/(c\,t)\}^{1/(t+k)} \rceil\).

current_n

The number of observations used.

risk and optimal_n are NA when the data are constant. Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE when current_n has reached optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), method, loss_A, cost_c, k, t, variance_unusable (TRUE when the data are constant, so that no scale has been estimated; the attribute has the same name in every procedure of the package), and notes. conf_level and width are NULL.

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_mr_nexp_mean_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

The location is estimated by the sample minimum \(X_{(1)}\), and the loss from \(n\) observations is $$A\,(X_{(1)} - \theta)^k + c\,n^t .$$ Here \(A\) prices a unit of estimation error raised to the power \(k\), and \(c\,n^t\) is the cost of sampling. Because \(X_{(1)} - \theta\) is exponential with scale \(\sigma/n\), the risk for a fixed \(n\) is $$A\,\Gamma(k+1)\,(\sigma/n)^k + c\,n^t ,$$ which is smallest at \(n^* = \{A\,k\,\Gamma(k+1)\,\sigma^k/(c\,t)\}^{1/(t+k)}\). The sequential rule replaces \(\sigma\) by \(U_n = \sum (X_i - X_{(1)})/(n - 1)\): sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) with $$n \ge \{A\,k\,\Gamma(k+1)\,U_n^k/(c\,t)\}^{1/(t+k)} .$$ The optimal_n row is the right hand side rounded up, and the risk row is the estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A\,\Gamma(k+1)\,(U_n/n)^k + c\,n^t\); both are evaluated at the current data.

The optimality is asymptotic. As the cost constant falls (so that \(n^*\) grows), the expected final sample size approaches \(n^*\) and the risk of the procedure approaches the minimum. In simulation (A = 500, c = 0.01, each combination of k and t equal to 1 or 2, scales 0.25, 1, and 3, the pilot of seq_mr_nexp_mean_pilot() with its defaults, 40,000 replications, Monte Carlo standard error at most 0.007), the ratio of the risk to the minimum was between 1.00 and 1.03 in ten of the twelve conditions, in which \(n^*\) ran from 18 to 387. The two exceptions both had k = 2 and t = 2: the ratio was 1.04 at scale 1, where \(n^*\) is 18, and 1.09 at scale 0.25, where \(n^*\) is 9 (400,000 replications each, standard error 0.002).

Data. Any finite values are accepted, because the location may be negative. The model is right skewed with a sharp lower endpoint; the function cannot check that.

Constant data. If every observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value), \(U_n\) is zero, or nothing but rounding error, and the rule as printed would be met at once. The function departs from the printed rule deliberately: no scale has been estimated, so the rule is reported as not met, risk and optimal_n are NA, attr(out, "variance_unusable") is TRUE, and a note says so (see smsd_check_methods); data whose real spread is that small beside their size should have a common value subtracted first.

Extreme units. Data that do vary, but whose spread is at the very edge of double precision, so that the scale estimate cannot be represented (differences among the observations near \(10^{308}\) or near \(10^{-323}\)), are an error that says to change the units. That case is not reported as a rule not yet met, because collecting more data cannot help.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_mr_nexp_mean_pilot; seq_fwd_nexp_mean for a fixed width confidence interval for the same location.

Other seq_mr_nexp_mean: seq_mr_nexp_mean_pilot()

Author

Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in, Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Shortest possible delivery time for an online retailer, in days. An
# error of one day is valued at 500 dollars and tracking one more order
# costs 0.25 dollars. Times are simulated here as a minimum of 2 days
# plus an exponential delay averaging 1.5 days, so the best sample size
# is sqrt(500 * 1.5 / 0.25), about 55.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_mr_nexp_mean_pilot(A = 500, c = 0.25, k = 1, t = 1)
days <- 2 + rexp(m, rate = 1 / 1.5)
out <- seq_mr_nexp_mean(days, A = 500, c = 0.25, k = 1, t = 1)
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (negative exponential location))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 7
#>   Criterion n     : 50
#> 
#>   location          : 2.15913
#>   risk              : 90.03639
#>   optimal_n         : 50
#>   current_n         : 7
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one order at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  days <- c(days, 2 + rexp(1, rate = 1 / 1.5))
  out <- seq_mr_nexp_mean(days, A = 500, c = 0.25, k = 1, t = 1)
}
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (negative exponential location))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 53
#>   Criterion n     : 53
#> 
#>   location          : 2.001436
#>   risk              : 26.17606
#>   optimal_n         : 53
#>   current_n         : 53
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
